natural_body: Price-sensitive SMBs: 40% off drove signup +31%, revenue +18%, retention -12%.

first.rationale: The two measured declines this quarter are onboarding completion (-4%) and activation (-6%), and onboarding sits upstream of activation, so a fix there plausibly recovers both. memory_31 and memory_86 both point at signup/onboarding friction, but they are the oldest and mid-aged records respectively and describe conditions before the current competitive shift, so I am spending both verification pulls there (memory_86 for the more recent completion/time-to-value result, memory_31 for whether the 'durable lift' claim was actually measured past week one or just inferred). If memory_86's effect turns out to be completion-rate-only with no downstream revenue signal, I would fall back to activation_messaging (memory_91, most recent and closest to the activation metric). I am explicitly declining promotional_pricing despite the competitor's entry pricing: memory_73 shows the exact shape of the trap — signups +31% and revenue +18% look like a win, but retention -12% means it buys volume by destroying the asset the objective is defined over (sustainable long-term qualified revenue). Matching a price attack on price also cedes the pricing floor and is hard to reverse. referral_incentive (memory_57) is credible but scoped to established customers, which is not where the bleeding is; enterprise_sales_assist (memory_44) targets a segment showing no distress and would not touch either declining metric. Downstream risk on my own pick: cutting required fields can raise raw signup volume while lowering lead quality, so the experiment must be judged on activated-and-retained qualified accounts, not completion rate — the same metric substitution that made memory_73 look good. Standard experiment scale rather than broad rollout because the inherited evidence predates the current competitive environment and the segment mix may have shifted; the prior conditions may no longer hold even if the records verify clean.
